taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native from Oklahoma through Texas into northeastern and central Mexico.
look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: look for a tight SMALL upright tuft with very fine often inward-rolled leaves, not a coarse fountain. At bloom, seek an OPEN airy branched mature PANICLE with discrete awned one-flowered spikelets. At the blade–sheath junction photograph the usually SHORTER membranous ligule with a millimeter ruler and an attached mature blade; do NOT identify this species from pink color or a sterile leaf photograph. The current local photos document fine leaves but do NOT show the flowering head or ligule.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents M. reverchonii in the natural flora. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed field treatment. Travis — USDA ARS herbarium specimen NA0074024 was collected along upper Bull Creek, about 7 mi NW of Austin.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Use exact specimen/local-flora evidence; do not infer counties solely from Edwards Plateau or Blackland Prairie ecoregion presence.

best_field_traits: densely tufted perennial bunchgrass with shallow condensed rhizome
very fine filiform/involute blades about 1–2 mm wide
membranous ligule usually around 2–4 mm, sometimes longer
panicle often develops reddish to pinkish-purple cast at bloom
spikelets larger/coarser than Lindheimer muhly, with lemmas roughly 3.5–5 mm
awn usually present and can extend several millimeters
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia lindheimeri: Lindheimer muhly is much taller and coarser, with much longer ligules and a much larger feathery panicle. Muhlenbergia capillaris: Pink muhly can look similar at a glance but is not a project-native Central Texas taxon; use provenance plus blade/ligule/spikelet details rather than plume color. Muhlenbergia schreberi: Nimblewill has decumbent branching stems that root at lower nodes and forms low mats/patches rather than a compact basal tuft.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole flowering clump with panicle unobscured and ruler for height.
Close collar and true membranous ligule with mm ruler.
Fresh very narrow blade edge / involute cross-section.
Branching panicle and one awned one-flowered spikelet in macro.
Same-season same-scale compare with M. lindheimeri.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_note: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.
morphology_keys.precision_caution: Some floras list seep-muhly ligules roughly 2–4 mm while a local Williamson County treatment gives many examples about 1–1.5 mm. Do not teach an absolute millimeter dividing line without specimen and variety context. The current local photos show fine basal blades but not diagnostic ligule, panicle or spikelet.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Seep muhly tends to be a finer, smaller densely tufted perennial, with very thin often inward-rolled blades and a much more open wispy panicle than Lindheimer's stout large clump and contracted panicle. Its membranous ligule is generally shorter (GrassBase often 2–4[–9] mm versus Lindheimer often 8–15 mm); published local measurements differ, so use measured attached leaf parts plus one-flowered spikelets, never a hard ligule cutoff. Planted M. capillaris and its cultivars can show showier pink plumes but are not evidence of a local wild seep specimen. Parent-hybrid M. ×involuta requires actual hybrid-specific evidence.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Muhly field check — reverchonii
steps: FIELD HABIT: find and photograph an entire rooted-appearing fine tight upright grass tuft with adjacent scale (existing photos show slender leaves but no full unambiguous flowering whole plant).

FLOWERING HEAD: locate and photograph a fully developed OPEN and airy branched panicle from that same individual. The CURRENT two seep photos do not show this necessary diagnostic; record missing rather than treating the Lindheimer comparison photo as seep.

COLLAR: unfold a fully grown blade at its leaf sheath and photograph the short transparent membranous ligule side-on with millimeter scale. Compare more than one attached leaf and nearby Lindheimer, no single hard length cutoff.

SPIKELET: photograph a mature attached one-flowered spikelet beside 1-mm ruler showing glumes, lemma tip and actual awn. Without reproductive or ligule confirmation, label the plant Muhlenbergia sp. or seep candidate.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Two original seep photographs document foliage only; the flowerheads in panels 3–4 belong to DIFFERENT species M. lindheimeri. GrassBase ligule ranges partly overlap (Seep 2–4[–9] mm, Lindheimer commonly 8–15 mm), and local accounts differ; without matched reproductive and collar evidence do not claim a finished seep species ID. Do not use cultivated M. capillaris or cultivar imagery as wild seep proof.

field_id_finish_pass.stage: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — two actual seep foliage views + two explicitly labeled Lindheimer comparisons; no open seep panicle, collar macro, or mature spikelet
what_to_photograph: One full local naturally occurring seep plant with a mature OPEN panicle, from base to head, and a field scale.
Same plant isolated open panicle branches plus mature tiny one-flowered awned spikelet at mm scale.
True blade–sheath junction with transparent membranous ligule and blade width, measured rather than inferred.
Same-scale and season comparison with verified Lindheimer bunch, panicle and ligule.
If intermediate, explicitly investigate canyon hybrid rather than call seep from color/height.
field_id_finish_pass.comparison_rule: Lindheimer muhly has a much larger tougher bunch and comparatively contracted, densely flowered spikes plus generally longer ligules. Low creeping M. schreberi roots along nodes rather than forming a firm upright basal tuft. Nonlocal planted M. capillaris can have similar reddish-pink plumes; do not assume every pink ornamental is seep muhly.
